title: The noob gains fallacy
summary: Argues that noob gains are not a time window you can 'waste' with a bad program, but a latent potential that stays until unlocked, and that they are compartmentalised by body part, so any muscle never trained before responds like a beginner's. He uses his own fast-growing triceps long head as proof, rejects a fixed natural limit, and wonders why former athletes seem to keep growing longer.

claims.claim: The idea that a bad program 'wastes your noob gains', as if starting to lift ignites a fixed time window, is nonsense.
Noob gains are a latent potential that stays in you and can be unlocked at any time in life; they are less potent if you start old, and best when starting right after puberty.
Anyone who has never lifted will experience noob gains as long as they have no hormonal deficiency.
A year on a bad program wastes a year but not your potential; someone who spent 6-8 months on a machine-only program will grow fast once switching to a compound-heavy program.
Noob gains are compartmentalised by body part: a muscle never trained (e.g. calves after 10 years of only thigh work) will still experience noob gains when you start training it.
His definition: noob gains are a muscle's ability to adapt very quickly to a stress it hasn't experienced before, adding size fast before tapering off.
Body-part-specific noob gains mean naturals will practically never meet their natural limit, since there's always another body part to work.
Despite being fairly advanced, he barely trained triceps, calves, traps and forearms before and is now getting noob gains on them.
He doesn't believe in the natural limit concept.
You might not be hitting a muscle the right way: lots of behind-the-head triceps extensions never grew his long head, but new exercises made it explode, giving him stretch marks in the armpits.
A lagging body part often isn't bad genetics but not having found the right way to stimulate it; an exercise that fails for one person can blow up another's muscle.
Noob gains are relevant for everyone, not only noobs.
In his country his football team had no gym, yet on their first gym visit a ~170 lb teammate cleaned about 205 lbs on his first try.

He observes that athletes who move to weightlifting experience noob gains again and often keep growing longer than others; he wonders whether their athletic background or something like myonuclei explains it.

exercises.name: Behind-the-head triceps extension
exercises.why: did lots of them but his long head never grew from them
